title: Chi-square goodness-of-fit
design: Each offspring is assigned to one of three genotypes.
data_characteristics: One categorical response with three mutually exclusive outcomes
other_examples: Mutation classes versus a predicted spectrum
question: Do the genotype frequencies follow the expected 1:2:1 segregation ratio?
null: Genotype probabilities are AA = 0.25, Aa = 0.50, and aa = 0.25.
options: Supply p in exactly the table’s category order.
Use counts as the first argument.
simulate.p.value = TRUE can calibrate sparse multinomial counts.
assumptions: Offspring are independent for the intended model.
Categories are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
Expected counts support the chi-square approximation.
parametric: Use a multinomial model when probabilities depend on predictors.
If null probabilities were estimated, account for fitted parameters.
nonparametric: Use Monte Carlo multinomial null simulation for sparse counts.
For only two outcomes, use an exact binomial test.

plot_args.note: Compare observed and expected counts side by side.

code_simulate:
set.seed(3104)
d <- data.frame(offspring = 1:240,
  genotype = sample(c("AA", "Aa", "aa"), 240, replace = TRUE,
                    prob = c(.18, .54, .28)))
write.csv(d, file.path(out_dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
code_plot:
par(mar = c(4, 5, 2, 1), las = 1)
bars <- barplot(rbind(Observed = observed, Expected = expected),
                beside = TRUE, col = c("#126887", "#d7d7d7"), border = NA,
                ylim = c(0, max(observed, expected) * 1.22),
                names.arg = names(observed), ylab = "Offspring", xlab = "Genotype")
text(bars, rbind(observed, expected), labels = c(rbind(observed, expected)),
     pos = 3, cex = .85)
legend("topright", c("Observed", "Expected under 1:2:1"),
       fill = c("#126887", "#d7d7d7"), bty = "n")
code_analysis:
observed <- table(factor(d$genotype, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa")))
fit <- chisq.test(observed, p = c(.25, .50, .25))
expected <- as.numeric(fit$expected)
departures <- observed / sum(observed) - c(.25, .50, .25)
practice: Would equal expected counts answer the same question as a 1:2:1 expected ratio?
generating_model: Independently sample 240 offspring genotypes with probabilities AA = 0.18, Aa = 0.54, aa = 0.28. Test against the fixed Mendelian probabilities 0.25, 0.50, 0.25; no probabilities are estimated for the null.
generating_truth: The simulated probabilities differ from 1:2:1 by -0.07, +0.04, and +0.03. The goodness-of-fit null is false.

columns.name: genotype
columns.meaning: AA, Aa, or aa genotype category

teaching_point: Expected counts encode the biological hypothesis. Equal expected counts would test a different hypothesis.
